extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and informed readers interested in architectural design and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on the form, function, and decoration of roof cornices, brackets, parapets, and buttresses—how these elements should be designed and when ornamentation becomes a fault. Emphasises structural truth, appropriate proportion, and the relation between form and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornice limited to the roof edge
rubrics_metrics.description: The architectural peroration or cornice is strictly and sternly limited to the end of the wall's speech, — that is, to the edge of the roof; and that it has nothing whatever to do with shafts nor the orders of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attach the roof-cornice to shafts or treat it as part of a column's shadow. The late Roman and Renaissance practice of cutting the roof-cornice to pieces and attaching bits to every column is condemned as a folly and a corruption of true principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornice family for military-derived roofs (bracket + parapet)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second family of wall cornices, derived from mediaeval military architecture, has two distinct features: first, the bracket; second, the parapet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing this cornice type, consider both bracket and parapet in succession; understanding both is necessary for knowledge of cornices, brackets in general, and balconies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket: prefer propped/deepened forms for security
rubrics_metrics.description: In military cornices the brackets are composed of long stones supporting each other in gradually increasing projection; the next step is to deepen the brackets so as to get them propped against a great depth of the main rampart, and to have small arches thrown from bracket to bracket to carry the parapet wall more securely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deepened-and-propped form is described as the most perfect: it satisfies the eye of security, gives full protection to the wall, and is applicable to all architecture. Use arches between brackets where practical; avoid forms that look insecure or 'giddy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracket strengthening methods and material suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A bracket may be strengthened in one of three ways: (1) by putting a second or third stone beneath it; (2) by giving it a spur; (3) by giving it a shaft and another bracket below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms a and c (simple projection or spur) are adapted for wooden buildings; b and d (stacked stones or shaft + lower bracket) for stone buildings. Beware that form d (shaft with bracket below) is often a Renaissance barbarism when scale/weight make it inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration must show insertion into the wall
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole power of the construction depends upon the stones being well let into the wall; and the first function of the decoration should be to give the idea of this insertion, if possible; at all events, not to contradict this idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorative details should reinforce the perception of structural truth. Anti-pattern: curling, detached ornament that avoids the wall (e.g., curling lines that make a bracket look pinned on and liable to slide) — a Classical/Renaissance fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parapet laws for non-military buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Respecting the parapet for mere safeguard upon buildings not military, there are just two fixed laws. It should be pierced, otherwise it is not recognised from below for a parapet at all, and it should not be in the form of a battlement, especially in church architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plain level parapet that the arm can rest upon is most comfortable. Use battlements only where their alternation of shadow is certain to be shown under most conditions and on a scale large enough to admit bold battlements; avoid diminutive/chopped battlements which are 'children's Gothic' and a falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use battlements only for shadow effect and appropriate scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the battlement consists in its letting shadow into the light of the wall, or vice versa; but the actual outline of a battlement by itself is an ugly succession of line unless used at a scale that preserves its origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply a castellated outline as mere ornament or to Gothicise unmanageable spaces; battlements must remain large enough to suggest their defensive origin, otherwise they are among 'the great idiocies of the present day.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Parapet ornamentation allowed where decorative purpose dominates
rubrics_metrics.description: Stone parapets, however pierced, are strong enough for protection and lighter forms may be admitted; flamboyant (lace-like) parapets and Arab-derived jagged finishings are decorative features and often preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where parapets are decorative rather than protective (e.g., Venetian examples, unroofed courts), more fantastic or intricate penetrations are acceptable and can enhance picturesque effect—especially when set off by roof materials that show contrast of light and shadow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buttress classification by function and force
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttresses divide broadly into those which meet and break the force before it arrives at the wall, and buttresses which stand on the lee side of the wall and prop it against the force. Lateral forces are of three kinds: dead weight, moving weight, and sudden concussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design buttresses in response to the type of lateral force: use prop buttresses for dead weight; parrying forms towards the attacking force for moving weight; and buttresses on both sides for concussions (or vibratory motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Buttresses against moving weight: set toward the weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttresses intended to guard against moving weight are set towards the weight they resist; they divide currents or parry forces before they reach the wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such forms are common in bridges, ship prows, or harbour piers but are rare in ornamental architecture; name and be aware of their place in the system though they are seldom used decoratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buttresses for vibratory motion: expand the base (pyramidal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttresses for vibratory motion resolve into expansion of the base of the wall so as to make it stand steadier; this pyramidal approach is useful in earthquake-prone regions and gives a heavy outline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these as ramparts or sloping bases where shocks or artillery action are concerns; examples include bastion/rampart profiles and certain southern/Egyptian slopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop (conducting) buttresses for dead weight: mass vs strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A prop buttress acts partly by its weight and partly by its strength. Mass buttresses resist by inertia (a heap of stones), while conducting buttresses convey the weight through their body to something else and must be of coherent, strong materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether mass or conducting action is appropriate. Conducting buttresses require careful cohesion and form; mass buttresses are less dependent on shape or cohesion but require sheer bulk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific buttressing: throw loads to points and minimise conducting forms
rubrics_metrics.description: As science advances, weights are deliberately thrown upon certain points; the directions and degrees of forces are exactly calculated and met by conducting buttresses of the smallest possible dimensions, supported by vertical buttresses acting by weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems of rods/channels where forces are divided and carried to ground efficiently; unnecessary bulk or misapplied repetition is to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinnacles: primarily decorative, use where they add stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pinnacles are often decorative; they give some weight but if weight alone were desired a lump of lead would suffice. Their natural and proper position is where they add to the stability of the building—on main wall piers and vertical buttress piers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pinnacles to reinforce vertical piers where they contribute materially to stability or as niches/statue settings; avoid their gratuitous application where they are merely ornamental or replaceable by safer, simpler weight solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flying buttress purity: visible prop with arch beneath
rubrics_metrics.description: The flying buttress in its purity is a mere sloping bar of stone (a prop or shore), with an arch beneath it to carry its weight — faithfully and visibly performing a humble office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep flying buttresses simple and honest. Piercing them with elaborate traceries or replacing early traceries with flamboyant ones can be effeminate, false in principle, and may weaken the structure. Ornament must not sacrifice security or clarity of function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit buttress application to clear service
rubrics_metrics.description: Buttresses are to be regarded with respect when their form is simple and their service clear; but their unnecessary and lavish application (as decorative breaks of blank surface) is a misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying buttresses out of laziness or vanity; do not use them merely to cover up wall deadness or to suggest sanctity. Misplaced buttresses (e.g., on trivial buildings or inside pews) are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose buttress system according to desired interior light
rubrics_metrics.description: The northern buttress system is based on the requirement for tall windows and vast light, using external buttresses. The Italian method fears light and makes walls wide enough between windows to bear the roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select northern external-buttress strategies when large interior light is desired and accept the exterior 'skeleton' effect; choose Italian thick-wall approaches when calm, solid exterior surfaces and less interior light are preferable. Both systems have merits in their proper place.
